title: useEffect
subtitle: Side effects — data fetching, subscriptions, timers, and cleanup
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: React components should be pure functions (same input → same output, no side effects). But real apps need side effects: fetch data from an API, set up a WebSocket, start a timer, update the page title.
whyItExists.solution: useEffect lets you run side effects after render. React calls your effect after the DOM is updated. You can specify when to re-run via the dependency array, and return a cleanup function that React calls before re-running or when the component unmounts.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Data fetching on mount or when dependencies change. DOM manipulation that can't be done via JSX. Subscriptions (WebSocket, event bus). Timers (setInterval, setTimeout). Syncing React state with an external system.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Transforming data for rendering — do it during render (not in an effect). Handling user events — use event handlers. Initializing state from props — do it in the initial value of useState.

explainModes.beginner: useEffect runs some code after the component renders. You give it a function (the effect) and a list of values to watch (the dependency array). If you pass an empty array [], the effect runs once when the component first appears. If you pass [userId], the effect re-runs whenever userId changes.
explainModes.simple: Three forms: useEffect(fn) — runs after every render. useEffect(fn, []) — runs once on mount. useEffect(fn, [dep1, dep2]) — runs when deps change. Return a cleanup function to cancel work: return () => clearInterval(id). Dependencies: anything from the component scope used inside the effect must be in the array. Async: don't make the effect function async — define an async function inside and call it.
explainModes.standard: The cleanup function runs: (1) before the effect re-runs (when deps change), and (2) when the component unmounts. This prevents leaks: cancel fetches, clear timers, remove event listeners. React 18 StrictMode runs effects twice in development to expose missing cleanups — this is intentional and means your cleanup must be correct. Data fetching pattern: inside effect, create an 'ignore' flag to cancel stale responses when the effect re-runs.
explainModes.technical: Effect timing: useEffect fires after the browser has painted. If you need to run synchronously after DOM changes (before paint), use useLayoutEffect — but this is rare and can cause visual jitter. Dependency lint rule: react-hooks/exhaustive-deps (from eslint-plugin-react-hooks) warns when deps are missing. Missing deps cause stale closure bugs. Extra deps cause the effect to re-run too often. AbortController: the modern way to cancel fetch requests. Create an AbortController in the effect, pass its signal to fetch, and call controller.abort() in cleanup.
explainModes.deepDive: The 'rules of hooks' apply to useEffect: same call order every render, no conditionals. Multiple useEffects per component are allowed and encouraged — separate concerns into separate effects. Event loop ordering: React batches DOM updates and calls effects asynchronously in a microtask (React 18) — effects run after the paint, so they never block the first render. Concurrent features: in concurrent mode, React may abort and restart renders. Effects only run after a render is committed to the DOM — they're guaranteed to see a consistent DOM state. Comparison to lifecycle methods: componentDidMount ≈ useEffect(fn, []), componentDidUpdate ≈ useEffect(fn, [deps]), componentWillUnmount ≈ the cleanup function.

questions.question: Why should you return a cleanup function from useEffect when using setInterval?
options: Cleanup functions are required by React for all effects — they're not optional
Without cleanup, the interval continues running even after the component unmounts, leaking memory and potentially calling setState on an unmounted component
The cleanup function is what starts the interval on the next render
Cleanup functions only matter for performance, not correctness
questions.explanation: setInterval schedules a recurring callback. If the component unmounts (e.g., user navigates away) without clearing the interval, it keeps firing — calling setCount or other state setters on an unmounted component causes a React warning (possible memory leak) and may cause bugs. The cleanup function (return () => clearInterval(id)) tells React to cancel the interval when the effect re-runs or the component unmounts.

faq.q: Why can't I make useEffect's callback async?
faq.a: useEffect's callback must either return a cleanup function or nothing. An async function returns a Promise — React would receive a Promise as the 'cleanup', which it doesn't know how to call. The fix: define an async function inside the effect and call it: useEffect(() => { async function load() { ... } load(); }, []).

examples: useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId).then(setUser); }, [userId]) — refetch on ID change
useEffect(() => { const sub = socket.subscribe(topic, handler); return () => sub.unsubscribe(); }, [topic])
useEffect(() => { const id = setTimeout(() => search(query), 400); return () => clearTimeout(id); }, [query]) — debounce
